summary:
The Australian Capital Territory stands under the Australian national framework. Its own Human Rights Act 2004 (A2004-5) is in force and is the statutory rights framework that territory public authorities must operate within. Section 31 permits an interpreter to consider international law and the judgments of foreign and international courts and tribunals relevant to a human right. The ACT Legislation Register records uncommenced amendments made by the Human Rights (Housing) Amendment Act 2025.

Conversion practices are banned under territory law. The Legislative Assembly passed the Sexuality and Gender Identity Conversion Practices Bill on 27 August 2020, and from early 2021 practices used on protected persons carry up to 12 months' imprisonment or a $24,000 fine. Civil penalties run alongside the criminal offence, and the ACT Civil and Administrative Tribunal can issue orders and order redress. The bill was amended before passage after the Association of Christian Schools and the ACT Law Society argued the definition of a conversion practice was too broad and vague; practices supporting a person who is undergoing or considering a gender transition are explicitly not banned.

Prison policy in the territory provides for explicit self-identification, with transgender prisoners housed according to their lived gender. A 2026 report by the Human Rights Law Centre, produced with the trans community organisations Flat Out and FIGJAM, documents strip-searching in Australian prisons including those in the ACT and records disproportionate harms for trans, gender-diverse and Indigenous prisoners.

Health care capacity is the territory's weakest point for trans visitors and residents. The ACT government's LGBTIQ+ Health Scoping Study, reported on 16 April 2022, found a shortage of primary-care professionals including GPs, of mental-health supports and of paediatric specialists with LGBTIQ+ health understanding, producing excessive wait times, delays from referrals and high costs associated with interstate and international travel. Twenty young transgender people were on the waitlist of Canberra's only paediatric endocrinologist, with some patients waiting a year for an appointment, and GP demand was rising by 20 to 40 per cent a year.
tangentialFactors:
The ACT is one of a small number of Australian jurisdictions whose prison policy explicitly provides for self-identification by transgender prisoners.

Gender care in the territory depends on cross-border movement: the scoping study records patients travelling interstate and overseas for treatment because local capacity is short, and it described the ACT as the only jurisdiction without a comprehensive gender-focused health service, whether in private practice or through a publicly funded gender clinic.
localsOnly:
Residents who experience a conversion practice can pursue civil redress: the ACT Civil and Administrative Tribunal may issue orders and order redress in addition to the criminal penalties of up to 12 months' imprisonment or a $24,000 fine.

People held in ACT custody are subject to the territory's self-identification housing policy for transgender prisoners, and the 2026 strip-searching report records disproportionate harms for trans and gender-diverse prisoners in ACT prisons.

Residents seeking gender care face the capacity shortfall documented in the scoping study: 20 young people on the waitlist for Canberra's only paediatric endocrinologist, waits of up to a year, and GP demand rising by 20 to 40 per cent a year.
outOfScopeNotes:
The health scoping study dates from 2022; current figures for ACT gender-care capacity and waitlists are not sourced.

The 2026 strip-searching report documents practice in ACT prisons, but ACT-specific findings, numbers or outcomes from it are not sourced.

The Human Rights (Housing) Amendment Act 2025 amendments to the Human Rights Act 2004 are recorded as uncommenced, and their commencement date is not sourced.

The conversion practices bill was amended before passage after objections that the definition was too broad and vague; the final statutory wording of the definition is not sourced.
